scribe_response.text: Tell me about someone who mattered a great deal in your life. The person who mattered most to me was my husband, Alan, husband Alan Hale. I met him in the autumn of nineteen sixty-nine, when I was a student nurse on Ward Six. His uncle Walter had fallen and broken a hip, and Alan, and Alan came every evening with a bag of mints. He was uh thin and tall, with round glasses and a pencil permanently behind his ear. On the third visit he left his um pencil, his pencil case on the locker, and I ran after him down the stairs. He thanked me so solemnly that I um laughed, um and he went pink to the tips of his ears. A week later he asked if I would like to see a bridge he had helped to draw. I said yes, and we spent a freezing Sunday looking at a footbridge in Wetherby. He explained every rivet to me, and I found that I enjoyed it. He was a draughtsman at a firm of engineers on Wellington Street, and he drew beautiful, careful lines. He was shy, he never raised his voice, and he had a dry humour that took a minute to arrive. My mother liked him at once, because he wiped his feet and admired her sewing. My father took longer, and tested him by asking about railway timetables. What happened next? Alan knew all of them, and my father shook um his hand with new respect. We married in June nineteen seventy-one um in the little chapel on Hollin Road. He drew the order of service himself um and decorated it with tiny swallows. We rented two rooms above a chemist's shop in Headingley and bought our first kettle together. He used to say that uh every good building begins with a good foundation, and so does a marriage. He cooked on um Saturdays, which meant beans on toast with a fried egg on top. Every Sunday afternoon he sat at the kitchen table and drew houses for fun. He would draw the house we might buy one day, with its garden and a little shed. When Helen was born in nineteen seventy-five, he held her as if she were made of glass. He sat up all night watching her breathe and drew her tiny hand on a scrap of paper. I still have that drawing, that drawing in a drawer, folded in tissue. As Helen um grew, he taught her to use a ruler, a compass and a sharp pencil. It was no surprise to either of us when she um decided to become an architect. Can you tell me more about that? He was never loud about being proud, but he kept her sketches in his wallet. When I worked nights, he was the one who waited up with tea and the newspaper. He never complained about the odd hours, my tired temper or the smell of antiseptic on my uniform. He had a way of listening with his whole face, which made you tell him everything. In his sixties he started to get tired, and then he began to get breathless. The doctors found a problem with his heart, and he went into hospital for tests. He was sent home with tablets and strict instructions, and he followed none of them. He built a bird table in the garden and fitted a little roof to keep the rain off. In the spring of two thousand and fifteen his heart stopped in the night, quietly, beside me. I knew before I woke fully, because the room felt different. I sat holding his hand until the light came up over the rooftops. People ask me how I coped, and I um tell them I went to the garden and pulled weeds. I think about him whenever I see a straight line or a well-made um joint. He taught me that quiet people can be the strongest, and that love is mostly paying attention.
